title: Command Responsibility, Individual Criminal Liability, and Modes of Participation
seo_title: Command Responsibility and Individual Criminal Liability in International Law
previous_article: Universal Jurisdiction and Accountability for Atrocity Crimes
next_article: International Criminal Tribunals, Hybrid Courts, and the Legacy of Nuremberg
excerpt: Command responsibility and individual criminal liability explain how international criminal law connects atrocity crimes to the people who plan, order, enable, commit, or fail to prevent them. This article examines modes of participation, superior responsibility, aiding and abetting, ordering, instigation, co-perpetration, indirect perpetration, common-purpose liability, joint criminal enterprise, omissions, mens rea, command authority, effective control, notice, failure to prevent or punish, and the evidentiary architecture needed to link accused persons to crimes. It distinguishes personal criminal responsibility from state responsibility and shows why atrocity prosecutions rarely depend on physical perpetration alone. The article also addresses Rome Statute Articles 25, 28, and 30, ICTY and ICTR jurisprudence, military and civilian superiors, fair-trial limits, defenses, and charging strategy. By combining doctrine, case studies, and lawyer-facing workflows, it shows how liability travels through institutions, command chains, and organized violence.
